title: Aeroflot 542
summary: An Aeroflot Lisunov Li-2 crashed into the Aradansky Range mountains shortly after takeoff from Abakan. The aircraft entered a descending turbulent air stream while flying through a mountain pass at low altitude. When pilots pulled the nose up to recover altitude the resulting high aerodynamic loads caused the left wing end fairing to collapse leading to loss of control and a dive into the mountainside.
probable_cause: The aircraft encountered descending turbulent air while flying through a mountain pass at low altitude. The pilots recovery action to pull the nose up caused excessive aerodynamic loads that the left wing end fairing was not designed to withstand. The structural design of the wing end fairing proved inadequate for the forces experienced during the recovery maneuver.

title: British European Airways 706 (1965)
summary: British European Airways Flight 706 departed from Edinburgh Turnhouse Airport at 23:17 on 26 October 1965 on a scheduled flight to London Heathrow. During approach to runway 28R with fog reducing visibility to less than 50 metres, the aircraft overshot the runway twice and entered a hold. On the final approach, the crew decided to overshoot with the nose up and reducing flaps. The aircraft crashed 2,600 feet from the threshold and burst into flames. Investigation attributed the crash to pilot error with contributing factors including low visibility, pilot fatigue, anxiety, lack of experience in fog landing, and procedural errors.
probable_cause: pilot error: incorrect flap selection, misjudged descent rate, and steep dive into runway during landing in fog below minimums

factors.evidence: the visibility at the time of the crash was significantly below the required minimum for landing with visibility less than 50 metres
pilot fatigue was a contributing factor noted in the investigation
the aircraft had performed two missed approaches before the crash
the final approach was marked by an incorrect flap selection and a misjudged descent rate
the aircraft crashed and burst into flames killing everyone on board

events.text: The aircraft departed from Edinburgh Turnhouse Airport at 23:17 on 26 October
During final approach to runway 28R the aircraft encountered fog with visibility less than 50 metres
The aircraft overshot the runway twice and then entered hold
On the final approach the crew decided to overshoot taking the nose up and reducing flaps
The aircraft crashed 2,600 feet from the threshold and burst into flames killing everyone on board

notes: investigation attributed crash to pilot error
multiple contributing factors identified in investigation

title: American Airlines 383
summary: American Airlines Flight 383, a Boeing 727 carrying 57 passengers and 5 crew, was cleared for a visual approach to Cincinnati on November 8, 1965 in deteriorating weather with low visibility. The aircraft descended more rapidly than it should have without either pilot noticing, descending to just 3 feet above the airport while still 3 nautical miles away. The aircraft flew into wooded slopes in the Ohio River valley and crashed. Only three passengers and one flight attendant survived.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the pilots' failure to properly monitor their altitude during a visual approach into deteriorating weather conditions.

factors.evidence: The aircraft flew into thick clouds and a thunderstorm; the approach controller was advised of precipitation just west of the airport.
Lights from the houses in the Ohio River valley, located 400 ft below the altitude of the airport, may have conveyed an illusion of runway lights.
The aircraft descended through 500 ft in the last 42 seconds before impact but pilots did not detect the descent; failure to properly monitor altitude.
The aircraft had descended to the level of 553 ft above the airport while it was still about 5 miles northeast of the airport and continued descending below minimums.
Aircraft flew into the wooded slopes of the valley 3 km north of the runway threshold and then exploded.

events.text: Flight contacted airline to report estimated arrival at Cincinnati at 19:05.
Flight cleared by approach controller for visual approach to runway 18 and advised of precipitation west of the airport.
Approach controller transferred Flight 383 to Cincinnati tower frequency.
Flight 383 received clearance to land on runway 18.
Aircraft descended through 500 ft in last 42 seconds and flew into wooded slopes 3 km north of runway threshold in poor visibility, impacted at 225 feet below runway elevation and exploded.

title: United Airlines 227
summary: United Airlines Flight 227 crashed short of runway 34L at Salt Lake City while conducting a high and fast unstable approach. The crew descended at approximately 2300 feet per minute, nearly triple the recommended rate, remaining 2000 feet above the normal glideslope at the outer marker. The captain rejected the first officer's attempt to add thrust with only seconds remaining before impact. The aircraft struck the runway with 4.7g vertical acceleration, rupturing fuel lines and causing post-impact fire that turned an initially survivable crash fatal, with 43 killed and 48 survivors.
probable_cause: Captain's bad judgment in conducting the final approach from a position too high and too close to permit descent at normal and safe rate, resulting in impact short of the runway.

factors.evidence: plane was 2000 ft too high at outer marker with 2300 ft per minute descent rate
first officer attempted to add thrust but captain brushed his hand aside and said not yet
captain had failed his initial jet transition training and failed annual instrument proficiency check
pressurized fuel ignited inside cabin during slide, turning survivable crash into fatal accident
aircraft impacted short of runway 34L

events.text: Plane began descent from 10000 ft at approximately 2300 ft per minute, nearly triple the recommended rate
First officer reached forward to advance thrust levers to increase thrust but captain brushed his hand aside
Captain moved thrust levers to takeoff power position but engines failed to respond properly, only seconds before impact
Aircraft impacted with 4.7g vertical acceleration, breaking off left main landing gear and forcing right main gear through fuselage, rupturing fuel lines
Pressurized fuel ignited inside cabin, turning initially survivable crash into fatal accident with many survivors severely burned

title: Aeroflot 99
summary: Tupolev Tu-124 operating scheduled service from Leningrad-Pulkovo to Murmansk descended through poor weather with snow and 1.5 km visibility on 11 November 1965. The pilots, misidentifying neighborhood lights as runway lights, continued descending below the glidepath and increased rate of descent. The aircraft struck frozen Lake Kilpyavr 273 meters short of the approach beacon and 2127 meters short of the runway. 32 of 64 aboard perished; many survivors sustained injuries.
probable_cause: Pilot disorientation and visual illusion from neighborhood lights mistaken for runway lights, combined with descent below the glidepath. Contributing factors included absence of glidepath approach lights and inadequate ATC monitoring of descent rate.

factors.evidence: Weather conditions deteriorated around the destination with snow, cumulonimbus clouds at 260 meters and visibility of 1.5 km
pilots descended below the glidepath but did not notice their mistake immediately. What the pilots thought were runway lights were actually lights from a neighborhood
pilot-in-command increased the rate of descent, and at 15:57 the Tu-124 crashed into the frozen Lake Kilpyavr while 273 meters short of the beacon
airport was not equipped with glidepath approach lights
air traffic controller had failed to warn the crew that their altitude was too low
crashed into the frozen Lake Kilpyavr

events.text: The flight departed Leningrad-Pulkovo Airport at 2:21 pm for Murmansk.
The air traffic controller instructed the flight to reduce altitude to 700 meters with a bearing for landing of 215 degrees.
The captain began a turn at 800 meters altitude, losing altitude quicker than anticipated.
The pilots mistook neighborhood lights for runway lights and increased the rate of descent thinking they had not descended enough.
The Tu-124 crashed into frozen Lake Kilpyavr 273 meters short of the beacon and 2127 meters short of the runway, losing the left wing and breaking in two.

title: 1965 Carmel mid-air collision
summary: TWA Flight 42 (Boeing 707) at 11,000 feet collided with Eastern Air Lines Flight 853 (Lockheed Constellation) at 10,000 feet near Carmel, New York. An optical illusion caused the Eastern first officer to believe both aircraft were at the same altitude, prompting a climb that put the Constellation on a collision course. TWA's left wing struck the Constellation's tail.
probable_cause: The first officer of the Eastern Air Lines Constellation experienced an optical illusion causing him to believe the aircraft was on the same altitude as the Boeing 707, leading him to climb and place the aircraft in a collision path.

factors.evidence: Due to an optical illusion, the first officer of the Super Constellation believed it was on the same altitude as the Boeing 707
The Super Constellation's crew immediately began climbing to escape what they thought was an imminent collision. Their climb however, put them on a legitimate path to collide with the other aircraft
The aircraft appeared to be converging rapidly at the same altitude
TWA Flight 42's left wing had struck the tail of the Constellation and both aircraft were out of control

events.text: TWA 707 approaching Carmel VORTAC at 11,000 feet, Eastern Constellation at 10,000 feet
Eastern first officer saw Boeing at 2 o'clock position, shouted 'Look out' and applied up elevator
TWA captain disengaged autopilot, applied hard right roll then reversed to left, both pilots grasped controls
Two shocks were felt and the Boeing entered a steep dive; the Boeing's left wing had struck the tail of the Constellation
TWA crew recovered from the dive, declared an emergency with New York Center
Eastern crew used throttles only to control aircraft, made emergency landing on Hunt Mountain in North Salem

title: 1965 Philippine Sea A-4 incident

location.name: Philippine Sea off Japan, 68 miles from Kikai Island

summary: A US Navy Douglas A-4E Skyhawk carrying a nuclear weapon was pushed overboard during a training exercise on the aircraft carrier USS Ticonderoga. The attack jet was being rolled from the number 2 hangar bay to the number 2 elevator when it went over the side. The pilot, Lieutenant Douglas M. Webster, the aircraft, and the B43 nuclear bomb were never recovered from the 16,000 foot depth.
probable_cause: Aircraft pushed overboard during carrier handling during training exercise. Specific cause of the push not explained in available sources.

factors.evidence: attack jet was pushed backwards over the side during training exercise
The pilot Douglas M. Webster was never recovered

events.text: A training exercise was ongoing aboard USS Ticonderoga with Attack Squadron 56.
The A-4E Skyhawk was being rolled from the number 2 hangar bay to the number 2 elevator.
The attack jet was pushed backwards over the side off the number 2 elevator.
The pilot Lieutenant Douglas M. Webster, the aircraft BuNo 151022, and the B43 nuclear bomb were never recovered from the 16,000 foot depth.

notes: Unusual carrier deck incident, not typical aviation accident
Nuclear weapon loss classified as Broken Arrow
Incident not disclosed until 1989

title: Japan Airlines 813
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 813, a Douglas DC-8 with 41 occupants, experienced an uncontained failure of its number one engine shortly after takeoff from San Francisco International Airport on 25 December 1965. The engine exploded violently and ejected debris that damaged hydraulic systems and the number two engine pylon. The crew declared a mayday and made an emergency landing at Oakland International Airport across the Bay, where the aircraft landed successfully with no injuries.
probable_cause: Failure of the operator to properly secure the torque ring on the low-pressure compressor during an engine inspection and overhaul conducted in August 1965, resulting in fatigue cracks and uncontained engine failure.

factors.evidence: fatigue cracks were found in the torque ring of the low-pressure compressor during overhaul at Japan Air Lines Tokyo factory in August 1965 and the ring was replaced
the outer casing of the No. 1 engine's low-pressure compressor had been shattered and separated from the engine, all stages of low-pressure compressor were destroyed
nearly half of the left aileron had been torn off by the explosion while hydraulic pipes and the No. 2 engine pylon were damaged by flying debris
aircraft successfully landed on Runway 29 at Metropolitan Oakland International Airport and none of the 41 occupants onboard were injured

events.text: Aircraft took off from Runway 01 at San Francisco International Airport
No. 1 engine exploded while climbing at 270 knots and 4,500 feet, aircraft vibrated violently and rolled to the left
Pilots immediately performed engine failure checklist, vibrations subsided, fire in No. 1 engine but not visible from cockpit, learned of fire through flight attendant report
Pilot declared mayday within a minute of engine explosion and requested emergency landing, lateral control becoming difficult and hydraulic pressure decreasing
Captain decided to head for Runway 29 at Metropolitan Oakland International Airport, more direct approach than returning to San Francisco
Aircraft successfully landed on Runway 29 with none of the 41 occupants injured
